explanation: The fox lived alongside people, may have been buried by them on purpose, and ate plant material like the humans did, even though wild foxes eat only meat. Together these clues suggest the fox lived closely with people, perhaps as a companion animal. Choice C fails because the text compares the fox's diet to the humans' diet and to wild foxes, not to jackals' diet.

The text says that combining sellers' own data with social media information makes demand forecasts much more accurate, which helps retailers meet demand without overstocking. Choice A states exactly that. Choice B is too broad: the text is about forecasting, not a revolution in how everyone views fashion.

The single origin hypothesis says ironworking began in Anatolia around 2200–2000 BCE and spread outward. But sites in Central Africa (Ôboui and Gbatoro) show ironworking as early as 2300–1900 BCE, about the same time, which suggests iron production may have arisen independently in both places. Choice C still assumes the technology came from Anatolia, which the early African dates call into question.

fix.passage: The single origin hypothesis of iron metallurgy posits that the craft originated in Anatolia (West Asia) circa 2200–2000 BCE before diffusing to other parts of the world, including Africa. Some proponents of the hypothesis argue that iron production technologies first arrived in North Africa through Carthage, where the earliest evidence of ironworking dates to approximately 800–600 BCE, before these technologies spread to sub-Saharan Africa over the following centuries. However, excavation of multiple sites on the Adamawa plateau in Central Africa conducted by Étienne Zangato and Augustin Holl uncovered evidence of iron workshops that may have been in operation as late as 900–750 BCE in Gbabari and as early as 2300–1900 BCE in Ôboui and Gbatoro. These findings suggest that ______

explanation: In the other experiments, more empty space (a low product-to-space ratio) made products seem more valuable. If an inexpensive store context moderates (weakens) this effect, spacing should matter a lot at Tiffany & Co. but only a little at Forever 21, which is what choice A describes. Choice B reverses the direction of the spacing effect, so it doesn't show the same effect being weakened.

The text explains that competition favors intelligence and large brains, and that the brain-to-body ratio shrank only while competition was low. So when populations grew and competition intensified, conditions would have favored larger brains relative to body size. Choice A gets it backward: the text links competition to brain size, not to body size.

Davis had to listen to unclear recordings over and over to write down the lyrics herself, which suggests that reliable transcriptions of the improvised lyrics didn't already exist. The other choices bring in comparisons (popularity, number of recordings, innovation) that the text never discusses.

Consumers want ever-faster delivery, while companies still struggle with last-mile delivery and each new fix (like drones) creates new problems. That suggests consumer expectations may be getting ahead of what companies can realistically provide. Choice D is unsupported: nothing suggests companies lack motivation; they are actively trying new solutions.

The text describes doubts from other writers and critics about Ngũgĩ writing in Gĩkũyũ, then shows that he went on to write dozens of acclaimed, widely translated works. Choice C captures that contrast between skepticism and success. Choice B is wrong because his first works were in English, not Gĩkũyũ.

The text notes that more people now use smartphones for surveys and that this may change how they interact with surveys; the study then found that PC and smartphone users differed in multitasking and completion. Choice D states this main point. Choice B is wrong because the text reports these differences; it doesn't say researchers are investigating why they occur.

The text explains that wild and lab studies each have advantages, and that when their results conflict, at least one study missed a relevant factor. Choice C sums up this balanced view: both approaches work, but each has weaknesses that can affect results. Choice D overstates the text, which says one or both studies failed, not necessarily both.

A banker lying awake for hours because of his tears and emotion clearly shows that he is very upset. The other quotations show him acting cautiously, listening in the night, or being delighted, none of which shows distress.

Choice D describes a repeating cycle: each new year arrives bringing high ambitions (anticipation), and each leaves a sigh linked to the past (regretful reflection). Choice C mentions regret over wasted time but shows neither the anticipation nor the repeating cycle.

If Morrison aimed to bring more Black writers onto Random House's list, we would expect the share of Black authors published by Random House to rise during her time as editor, which is what choice A describes. Choice D shows she influenced style, but says nothing about which authors were published.

The text says the doctors' expertise wasn't ignored but was outweighed by the messengers' experiential relevance. Choice C fits: former volunteers had gone through the very experience participants were considering, and that mattered more than the doctors' credentials. Choice D contradicts the text by saying participants were skeptical of the doctors' expertise.

Moss needs some sunlight but risks drying out with too much. Since moss under the semitransparent quartz grew much longer shoots, the quartz likely let through enough light while lowering its intensity, helping the moss hold on to moisture. Choice B contradicts the result: if the quartz blocked needed light, the moss wouldn't grow better.

The claim is that the number of young Hawaiian speakers has grown thanks to ‘Aha Pūnana Leo. Choice A shows a jump from fewer than fifty child speakers when the school was founded to more than 2,000 student speakers at the school today. The other choices give population or language facts that say nothing about how many young people speak Hawaiian.

The text says Wagner added more horns, trombones, and tubas so that more instruments played at once, making key moments extremely loud. The other choices describe venues, concert halls, or singer training, which the text never mentions.

Social buffering means the presence of another member of the species reduces stress, and the study measures stress as the percent change in heart rate. Choice A shows lower stress with a companion snake than when alone or with a rope (which controls for simply having an object nearby). Choice C uses baseline and peak rates rather than the percent change the researchers used as their stress measure.

The claim has two parts: fermentation improves digestibility (less soluble fiber and raffinose) and nutrition (fewer antinutrients like tannins and trypsin inhibitors). Choice B shows reductions in both. Choice A shows more antinutrients in fermented beans, which would weaken the nutrition part of the claim.

Gift giving in this culture signaled and conferred social status, and craft guild members were highly discerning producers and consumers of material goods. So gifting finely made objects to such expert peers would likely have showcased skill and boosted a member's professional reputation. Choice D compares status across types of guilds, which the text gives no basis for.

The period is the time between pulses, and J0614-03 has the smallest period in the table, 0.136 seconds. Choice C is wrong because J1654-2335's period (0.545 s) is not the longest, and choice D fails because J0103+54's period is under one second.

With the ranking, participants spent 36% of their time on the top-ranked British Museum, far more than on any other museum and double the 18% spent by the unranked group. That supports the idea that people focus on the top-ranked option. Choice A describes only the unranked group, so it shows nothing about how rankings affect focus.

fix.passage: Researchers recently conducted an experiment to understand how we use rankings to make decisions. They created a fictitious travel website describing five museums in London. Then, they invited two groups of participants, who had never visited the museums, to review the site and select the museum they would be most likely to visit. Meanwhile, the researchers tracked the amount of time each participant spent reading about each museum. For one group, the website ranked each museum, titling the page “The Top 5 Museums in London.” For the other group, the museums and their descriptions were not ranked. The researchers concluded that when reviewing ranked lists, we tend to focus on the top-ranked option.

explanation: If the cost of traveling to market is high but stays about the same no matter how many goods are brought, then making fewer trips with more goods spreads that cost over more items and raises profit per unit sold. That explains why selling less often could be a strategic choice. Choice A describes a percentage fee, which costs the same per unit no matter how often goods are sold.

Mrs. Ochiltree makes startlingly frank comments about her acquaintances, and this causes people to avoid her, which suggests they are offended by what she says about them. Choice B is wrong because she actually enjoys being avoided, so she isn't missing their company.

The text says the linocut process let Catlett's work reach a wide audience and supported her aim to unite Black women through art. Choice B restates that. The other choices make claims about materials, commercial success, or being first that the text never makes.

The claim is that giraffes hum to communicate when they can't signal visually. If giraffes hummed only at night, when they couldn't see one another, that would directly support the claim. Choice A is about giraffe vision in general and says nothing about when humming occurs.

Mostly fine mudstone, which settles out of low-flow water, points to a long-lasting lake; cracks from episodic desiccation show the lake sometimes dried; and intervals of sandstone, deposited by flowing water, point to periods with streams. Choice B combines all three. Choice D says the lake never dried, which contradicts the desiccation cracks in the fine-grained mudstone.

The text says the researchers measured surprise by the cats' ear and head movements. The other choices describe strangers' voices, interacting with owners, or moving around the room, none of which is mentioned.

The parents find the house ordinary and inconvenient, but the children, after two years in London, see it as a Fairy Palace in an Earthly Paradise. Choice A captures this contrast. Choice B reverses who likes the house.

If categorizing pottery takes time away from important tasks that only human experts can do, then a model that handles categorizing would free archaeologists for that work rather than replace them. Choice A shows the model is faster, which, if anything, makes replacement seem more likely.

The AACM supports young artists with experienced mentors, and many organizations give similar support to young painters, writers, and other artists. This suggests many arts organizations see value in mentorship for young artists. Choice D compares the importance of mentors across art forms, which the text doesn't support.

Recovering a resin model destroys the burrow, so a burrow can be cast only once. That makes it impossible to record measurements throughout the burrow-building process, as the CT scanner can. Choice D may sound plausible, but the text says the problem is destroying the burrow, not distorting the resin.

The text says each planet's rotational period equals its orbital period. The table gives TRAPPIST-1e an orbital period of 6.1 days, so its rotational period is also 6.1 days. Choice D wrongly uses the planet's radius (0.92 Earth radii) as a rotational period.

explanation: Males prefer green females as mates, so blue plumage doesn't help females attract mates; however, males are less aggressive toward blue females when competing for resources. That suggests blue plumage in females persists for reasons other than mate attraction, such as avoiding aggression. Choice B predicts a specific future percentage that the text gives no basis for.

fix.passage: As juveniles, all white-necked jacobin hummingbirds display vibrantly blue head plumage; when they enter adulthood, males retain these blue feathers and most females molt to a drab green hue. However, 28% of adult female jacobins remain identical in coloration to juveniles and adult males. Based on field observations in Panama, a team of researchers reports that while adult males show a clear preference in mate selection for adult females with drab green feathers, they also engage in more antagonistic behavior toward those adult females than toward blue-feathered adult females when competing for resources. Therefore, the team hypothesizes that ______

explanation: Wood type can't explain the special sound, since modern violins use the same woods, but the old wood shows signs of chemical treatment. So the researchers likely suggest that this treatment helps explain the sound. Choice C contradicts the text, which rules out wood type as the explanation.

The sentence describes something that happened repeatedly over the decades: new calculations kept producing more precise coordinates, yet the meridian stayed put. Again and again fits this repeated pattern. Specifically doesn't work because the sentence doesn't detail the original method, and Granted would concede a point that the text never argued against.

The notes say the team wanted to better understand the mechanics behind nests' flexible yet cohesive structure, which is the aim of the study. Choice A states that aim. Choice B describes methods and choice C describes a finding, not the aim.

The soldiers' work was overlooked for decades, and then, in 2017, lawmakers finally recognized it. Then marks this next step in time. Lastly would suggest the end of a list, and For example would wrongly present the 2017 recognition as an example of being overlooked.

Calling himself Anglo-African is one way Coleridge-Taylor emphasized his mixed ancestry; using traditional African sounds in his compositions is another. In addition correctly adds a second example. However and Regardless signal contrast, but the two sentences agree.

fix.passage: Samuel Coleridge-Taylor was a prominent classical music composer from England who toured the US three times in the early 1900s. The child of a West African father and an English mother, Coleridge-Taylor emphasized his mixed-race ancestry. For example, he referred to himself as Anglo-African. ______ he incorporated the sounds of traditional African music into his classical music compositions.

explanation: Dove sets Thomas's story against the Great Migration, and she does the same with Beulah's story and the Civil Rights Movement. Similarly signals this parallel. Thus would wrongly suggest that the second point is a result of the first.

The study complicates the idea that dust bowl migrants mostly moved to California by showing that they more often simply relocated within their own region. More often captures this comparison. For this reason and additionally fail because the clause explains the complication rather than resulting from it or adding a separate point.

For an audience that already knows the magazine, the sentence should introduce the book itself: its author, title, and subject. Choice A does this. Choices B and C spend space explaining the magazine, which this audience already knows, and choice D focuses on one author rather than the book.

Choice C points out what the two specimens have in common: both belong to the genus Tyrannosaurus. Choice D highlights a difference (where they are housed), and choices A and B describe only one specimen.

An overview should explain what the process does and how it works. Choice B states that it makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen using an iron catalyst and high temperatures and pressures. Choice A lists ingredients without saying what the process produces, and choice D leaves out what the process makes.

An audience familiar with eDNA doesn't need it defined, so the best choice presents the study directly: who did it, where, and what they looked for. Choice A does this. Choices C and D spend space defining eDNA, and choice B doesn't mention the study at all.

Choice A describes the rocking chair (walnut, sleek contoured armrests and seat, in Boston's Museum of Fine Arts) and briefly identifies Maloof as an American woodworker for readers who don't know him. Choice D describes the chair but never says who made it, and choices B and C barely describe the chair.

Choice A names the study's leader and gives its finding: 74 Orchidaceae species in Oaxaca's temperate forests. Choice D describes the study but leaves out the finding, and choices B and C give the finding without presenting the study.

The researchers suspected aggressive behavior, but they found the opposite: the spiders are gentle and freeze when disturbed. Instead signals that what they found replaced what they expected. Therefore would wrongly make the gentle behavior a result of their suspicion.
Choice A emphasizes distance by giving the road's length (sixty-two miles) and the two cities it connected. The other choices focus on its status as a private turnpike or on when it was built.

Choice B names the food with the most magnesium, chia seeds at 150 mg/oz, and notes that this is more than peanuts and almonds. Choice A compares only almonds and peanuts, so it never identifies the highest.

The second sentence restates and explains what the split between dispersalists and vicariancists means. That is introduces this clarification. Furthermore and Similarly would treat it as a new or parallel point, and By contrast signals a contrast that isn't there.

Selenium was isolated in the same year it was discovered, while molybdenum took three more years to isolate. By contrast marks this difference. Similarly and For instance would wrongly suggest the two cases match.

Most known exoplanets orbit Sun-like G-type stars, but KELT-9b orbits a much hotter B-type star. However signals this contrast. For example fails because KELT-9b is an exception, not an example of the general pattern.
Choice C names both groups and states what they shared: transmitting coded military messages in their native languages. Choice D points out a difference, and choices A and B mention only one group.

The letter was addressed to a merchant, but Bolívar's real, final aim was to persuade English and European leaders. Ultimately (paired with though) conveys this underlying goal. Consequently and accordingly would wrongly make his goal a result of addressing the letter to Cullen.

The second sentence gives precise details (pauses of about 120 ms vs. 200 ms in human speech) that back up the general claim about pace. Specifically introduces these details. As a result would wrongly treat the pause lengths as a consequence of the discovery.

Hammurabi conquered Mesopotamia and built up Babylon, yet today he is mainly remembered for something else, his code of laws. However marks this contrast. Therefore and for instance wrongly suggest a cause-effect link or an example.

Choice B explains the benefit of the archive being online: it gives scholars more access to the documents without removing them from their home countries. The other choices describe the archive's size, contents, or director without pointing to an advantage of being digital.

Choice B states the disadvantage: audio-feature algorithms may misidentify the main features of songs with varying acoustic traits, making them less reliable. Choice A just describes the algorithms, and choices C and D focus on the strength of descriptive tags rather than the weakness of audio features.

The first sentence says the Inca recorded countable information with quipus; the second adds that they may also have recorded more complex information. In addition fits this added point. For example fails because stories aren't an example of countable data.

Choice A explains how fabric is used in the painting: the figures' clothing is made of fabric pieces stitched to the canvas. The other choices describe the exhibition or the figures without mentioning fabric.

The first sentence gives one concern about televising arguments (participants performing for cameras), and the second gives another (viewers seeing only misleading clips). Additionally adds this second reason. For example fails because the second worry isn't an example of the first.

The first sentence says Latimer improved Edison's light bulb design; the next explains exactly how, by placing cardboard around the filament to make it more durable. Specifically introduces this detail. Soon would wrongly suggest a later, separate event.

Choice B ties the declaration to Valle's change of beliefs: he long opposed independence, changed his mind after the 1820 revolt, and then wrote the 1821 declaration. Choice A leaves out the declaration, choice D leaves out Valle's beliefs, and choice C wrongly ties his change of mind to the 1814 repeal.

The first sentence says McFerrin finds research rewarding; the second strengthens this by saying she finds it as fascinating as visiting places in person. In fact introduces this stronger, emphasizing statement. Likewise would suggest a separate, parallel idea rather than an intensification.

Choice A both defines a Lazarus species (a living species once thought to be extinct) and names the mountain pygmy possum as an example. Choice B gives the example without defining the term, and choice D describes the idea without naming the term or giving an example.

The second sentence describes what scientists believed before Ramón y Cajal's 1873 finding, so Previously correctly places it earlier in time. However is tempting, but the first sentence already says the finding went against earlier assumptions; this sentence simply explains what those assumptions were.

Choice D states the advantage: the new catalyst stays highly effective while needing far less of the rare and expensive metal. Choice B contradicts the notes, and choices A and C describe platinum or typical catalysts without stating an advantage.

The first sentence says natural selection was an obvious next step given the ideas of the time; the second draws the logical consequence that it's not surprising two scientists reached it independently. Then signals this conclusion. However would wrongly suggest a contrast.

The first sentence says results have been impressive overall; the second backs this up with a claim that holds in many, though not all, instances: the bacteria have outperformed chemical cleaning. In many cases signals this. As a result fails because the bacteria's effectiveness isn't caused by the impressive results; it is what makes them impressive.
After fifteen years of resubmitting the bill, it at last passed in 1983. Finally signals the end of this long effort. Instead and Additionally don't express that this was the long-awaited result.

The long-held view is that humans arrived about 13,000 years ago, while the new research suggests over 30,000 years ago. However signals this contrast. Similarly and As a result wrongly suggest agreement or cause and effect.

Actors' self-awareness responses were suppressed when their names were called during performances but were normal outside acting. Conversely marks this opposite situation. Likewise would wrongly suggest the two results were the same.

As the population grew, the single district struggled, and eventually the court was split into two districts. Ultimately signals this final outcome of the growing problem. Nevertheless would wrongly suggest the split happened despite the struggles rather than because of them.

Choice A contrasts the two fabrics directly: Dhaka muslin is handmade with a very fine weave, while sheeting muslin is machine made with a coarse weave. Choice B only says they are different, and choice D describes just one muslin.
Choice D states what the two works share: both are LED light sculptures by Grimanesa Amoros. Choices A and B emphasize differences (texture and size), and choice C describes only Uros Island.

Choice D directly contrasts the two lever types by where the fulcrum and load are placed. Choice B mentions a difference vaguely without saying what it is, choice A doesn't mention the lever classes, and choice C states a similarity.

Choice A highlights a difference between the books themselves: Equiano's is an autobiography, while Sinclair's is fiction. Choice C points out different laws rather than a difference between the books, and choices B and D focus on similarities.

The movement had been explained as passive drifting with water currents, but the barnacles were found moving against the water flow, toward the turtle's head. That undermines the passive-drift explanation. Choice A is tempting, but the finding doesn't contradict the movement itself; it contradicts the explanation for it.

The first part says Siletz stories support the belief about the shipwreck; the next sentence gives a specific example, stories of beeswax (the ship's cargo) washing ashore. For example introduces this illustration. For this reason would wrongly make the beeswax stories a result of the belief.
